title: Load bank pilot circuit
goal: Reads like a control schematic: contacts and coils in recognisable positions, no wire crossing a symbol.

rubric.must: No wire passes through the inside of a component symbol.
Every component terminal that the netlist connects has a visible wire reaching it.
Wires run horizontally or vertically, with corners rather than diagonals.
Each reference designator and value sits beside its own symbol.
No two pieces of text overlap, and no text is crossed by a wire.

ideal.notes: Third pass. Fixes the engine's colliding selector label and sideways ground, gives every branch an even column pitch so no name touches a neighbour, and routes the left feed behind the control chain so nothing crosses.

audit.reviewedBy: a practising electronics engineer checking a schematic before layout

findings.what: The bare LED branches have no automotive transient or reverse-voltage protection.
findings.why: Series resistors limit forward current but cannot prevent LED reverse breakdown or excessive current during supply surges. The 15 A fuse will not protect these branches. Automotive supply protection requirements are described in [TI’s application note](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/snva681a/snva681a.pdf).
findings.fix: Add appropriately rated reverse-polarity protection and automotive transient suppression after F1, with the clamp voltage coordinated to the LED branches’ limits.

findings.what: LED current and resistor power ratings are not specified for the vehicle’s charging voltage.
findings.why: At 14.4 V with a 2 V LED, each 500 Ω branch draws 24.8 mA and dissipates 0.31 W while illuminated. That exceeds a 20 mA LED rating and a 0.25 W resistor’s continuous rating; flashing requires checking pulse ratings rather than assuming it is safe.
findings.fix: Specify LED and resistor ratings against the maximum operating voltage. For ordinary 20 mA LEDs on a supply reaching 14.4 V, use at least 680 Ω, 0.5 W for R1, R2, R4 and R5; also specify R3’s power rating.
